decision: The driver is built in Rust (portable-pty, a vt100 screen model, rmcp for MCP), offered as a command, as scenes in CI, and as an MCP server.
rejected: Adopting a Python MCP server; driving tmux (an extra program between, and a coarser screen); screenshots and vision for terminals (heavy, and text is already there).
why: Whatever ships is Rust; the pieces exist; the Python servers found show the design.

decision: The project is called agent access.
rejected: mcp-oco (names one protocol, not the purpose); agent-bridge (vague); tui-driver (one of its parts).
why: It says the purpose plainly: every tool usable by agents.

decision: lab-agent is delivered by the package conveyor (linux-package-distribution-oco/conveyor@v1); it keeps only its declaration, build scripts, PKGBUILD, public key and install test.
rejected: Keeping its own copy of the delivery machinery.
why: Its delivery workflows were a near copy of snapall's; copies drift and fixes do not travel.

decision: lab-agent records each wait itself - start, end, what is waited on, the project - and requires both on a waiting submit; a gatherer brings the waits into each project's data.
rejected: Logging waits by hand (it would be skipped); estimating them afterwards.
why: Capture must be unavoidable and cost nothing: the place every wait happens is lab-agent's own wait.

decision: A release tag is moved only after the change has landed and main is shown to hold it.
rejected: Tagging in the same breath as landing.
why: A job moved v1.0.1 after its change had been refused, so the tag claimed a fix it did not hold.

decision: Projects call the conveyor's reusable workflows, pinned to a version; nothing is copied into them.
rejected: A template repository; copy-paste with care; composite actions alone (they cannot hold whole jobs).
why: snapall and lab-agent carry about 500 lines of nearly identical workflow each; copies drift and fixes do not travel.

decision: The extraction is proven by moving snapall and lab-agent onto the conveyor with byte-for-byte the same published repositories - same URLs, same keys.
rejected: Proving it on a new project first.
why: An extraction that changes what users receive cannot be told from a regression.

decision: 'Nothing changed for users' means the same addresses and key, every signature verifying, and the README's install line installing the new release - not byte-identical packages.
rejected: Byte-for-byte identical repositories (the earlier wording of this decision).
why: Arch packages built twice differ in their timestamps; the byte promise could not be kept and would test nothing a user meets.

decision: Each project keeps its own signing key for now; one key for the whole commons is considered later.
rejected: One organisation key from the start.
why: A single key would change the trust of every existing installation at once.

decision: The conveyor's direction is to build in the project's own Nix environment (the shell.nix the lab machine uses), from Nix's binary cache; the patient retry stays as a fallback meanwhile.
rejected: Only retrying; switching to another single distribution's mirrors.
why: The author asked whether we must rely on Ubuntu's archive; Nix gives one pinned toolchain for the lab and CI, from a more robust source.

decision: A project describes its delivery in one small declaration file; the workflow inputs stay few.
rejected: Workflow inputs only.
why: Inputs grow without limit and are scattered across callers; a file is read, reviewed and checked like data.

decision: The conveyor's scripts live inside its workflows, not as files it fetches.
rejected: A scripts folder checked out at run time.
why: A called workflow does not know which version of itself was called, so fetched files could drift from the workflow; inline, they move together with the tag.

decision: Arch (pacman) and Alpine (apk, for postmarketOS) first, each with a signed repository.
rejected: Debian and RPM repositories first - installation on them stays verified, as today.
why: These are what the lab, the desktops and the phone actually run.

decision: The declaration is read by a typed Rust reader that refuses unknown fields, not by Python inside the workflows.
rejected: Python's tomllib inline (the first version); a shell TOML parser.
why: Shipped code that other projects call: with Python a misspelled field is silently replaced by a default - a bug Rust's types rule out by design. Asked by the author: no Python for new things.

decision: Cutting versions stays with each language's own tool (release-plz for Rust); the conveyor starts from a release tag.
rejected: The conveyor owning versions.
why: Versioning is part of a project's own decisions and tooling.

decision: devlab kernel install refuses a kernel that is not an EFI executable.
rejected: Documenting which file to pass.
why: The bootloader starts EFI programs only; a gzip kernel was lost before it could log a line.

decision: devlab health waits until the phone has been up 90 seconds before checking, saying so once.
rejected: A fixed sleep in every script; checking at once and retrying failures.
why: Every job slept before a health check by hand (7 times); a check read too early fails for the wrong reason.

decision: A listening test runs only with --placed, the word that the microphone is by the phone.
rejected: Un-naming the microphone's file as the safeguard: a trick only its author remembers.
why: The first results came from a microphone being worn.

decision: devlab kernel try waits for a new boot id and reports the outcome itself, judged from the running release, the entry's counter and the timeout log.
rejected: Waiting for the phone to go down and then up (it misfired twice: the try schedules its reboot); leaving the reading to a person.
why: Booting a test kernel and reading what happened was the heaviest manual work (9 times, 54 effort-minutes), and guessing at it cost three reboots.

decision: Test kernels are booted from their EFI image (vmlinuz.efi), and the conveyor refuses anything else.
rejected: Sort keys, a stored default entry, a second boot partition - each checked and ruled out.
why: A gzip kernel was chosen by the bootloader, counted down, and could not start - silently, before any log.

decision: The audio pin driver's function slots for the SoundWire pins follow the phone's own Android kernel (gpio19 swr_tx_data in slot 3, gpio23 swr_rx_data in slot 2).
rejected: Treating the clocks switching off as the cause; changing the macros' autosuspend.
why: A bus clash on the TX bus came right before the codec's timeout; the driver's table disagreed with the vendor's pin description on exactly these pins; corrected, the codec came up on the first boot.

decision: Boots that come up without the sound card are measured over a run of reboots before anything is changed.
rejected: Unmasking the helper service masked for the suspend crash, on a hunch.
why: It happened once in several boots; the audio processor's service channel never appeared. A guess at a cause would be untestable without a rate.

decision: With the SIM in, the modem is examined read-only first; switching the radio on is the only change made, and nothing that calls, messages or uses data happens without the author's word.
rejected: Trying a call or a data connection straight away.
why: A SIM card costs money and reaches people; the phone's state stays known.

decision: The capture failure is not chased in runtime power management.
rejected: Changing the macros' autosuspend or the controller's clock-stop handling.
why: With the bus controllers, macros, codec and SoundWire devices all forced awake, the read failure came at the same moment, the same way.

decision: The right channel is the bottom speaker.
rejected: An earlier 2 dB lean, taken while the microphone was not yet placed.
why: With the microphone at the bottom speaker the right channel read 7 dB louder (-20.4 against -27.6 dBFS; room -85.7).

decision: Where the community's report and our measurement disagree, both are shown side by side; where we know nothing, the report is shown outlined, dated, as reported.
rejected: Hiding a report behind our measurement; filling unknowns as if measured.
why: A disagreement is the most telling part of the comparison - the sensors one may be of our own making.

decision: Telephony is checked in three modes: automatic now (registration; a small download over mobile data), half-manual (the phone calls the author's other phone, the author confirms through the inbox), and fully automatic later (a two-phone stand, or a number that answers with a tone). The number to call lives in a private file on the lab machine, never in a repository.
rejected: Calls by hand without a check; keeping the number in the device manifest.
why: The author allowed data and calls to his other phone, and asked that the checks become part of the test suite so a stand can run them unattended.

decision: ocoeco check reads a project's essence as advice and never fails on a gap.
rejected: Failing the check until every step is served.
why: A gap is the truth about a project, not an error in its data.

decision: Code is changed by structure: whole items replaced with ast-grep, matched by their signature; logic kept outside macros where tools and readers see it; new views and tools added as new files; every edit verified before anything lands.
rejected: Text patches with better anchors; Comby (language-agnostic, less exact for Rust); writing our own rewriter.
why: Patching source by matching text was the heaviest manual work (19 times) and the cause of most failed runs, one of which landed a commit that changed nothing.

decision: Hand-work saturation is measured in effort - minutes weighted by load on Borg's CR10 scale - as well as count; there is no deliberate status: looking, listening and deciding are counted and automatable like the rest.
rejected: Count alone; NASA-TLX's six ratings on every bump (too heavy); exempting judgment from automation.
why: The author's 30 kg box: ten seconds, yet draining. And tests must judge sound and pictures themselves, with no person judging mid-run (jidoka).

decision: Hand-work becomes part of ocoeco's language: a handwork table of atomic actions with counts, recorded by ocoeco hand (match, bump, or ask), shown by the observatory as hand-work worth a tool.
rejected: Logging whole tasks (they never repeat); free-text notes in the session log (they cannot be counted); bumping on any resemblance without asking (silent merging of different actions).
why: Proposed by the author. A board task is many steps and never repeats; atomic actions do. The wording is kept from drifting by the tool, as the vocabulary keeps words from drifting.

decision: ocoeco check names every table a repository keeps beside its exported ones but does not export.
rejected: Exporting every file automatically - some are kept for a project's own use.
why: A device lab's whole backlog and a tool's decisions and log went unseen by the observatory for days; ocoeco note found it by refusing.

decision: Hand-work is called manual work everywhere - the table manual_work, the command ocoeco manual, land --manual; every record and bump appends a timed event to manual_events.
rejected: hand-work (less plain); ocoeco did (the person does, not the tool); inventing times for the history recorded before.
why: The author: manual work is the plain word, and with the time kept it can be set beside commits and releases. A command named manual could be read as documentation; the vocabulary defines it, and ocoeco has no documentation command to collide with.

decision: Rows are recorded with ocoeco note, not hand-written per job.
rejected: A per-job script; a general JSON editor that knows nothing of the format.
why: Every job wrote its own script to patch JSON: the same handwork again and again, each a chance to break a table. On its first use the tool found that ocoeco itself exported no decisions.

decision: ocoeco manual without an action opens a list in the terminal (ratatui): type to narrow, arrows, Enter, the usual minutes and load offered.
rejected: A web form (not TTY-first); fuzzy matching on typed text alone (it guesses).
why: Asked by the author: typing an action again is a chore and splits the ledger into near-duplicates.

decision: Research joins the language as its own table (question, found, sources, date); decisions cite it and name the steps they are about; the observatory badges each step with its decisions.
rejected: Sources alone (a list of works says nothing of the question asked); a separate research page with no link to steps.
why: Asked by the author: research should back decisions visibly, beside the milestones and progress they concern, and looking around should be a practice for agents and humans alike.

decision: Any row may be researched rather than live: it cites a research entry and is drawn outlined, with its age and a link; research gains versions (topic, date, supersedes), a refresh horizon, and a place in the attention view when it goes stale.
rejected: Copying outside claims in as if measured; overwriting research on refresh; marking live data (live is the default).
why: Asked by the author, to fill the picture honestly with what others achieved.

decision: Vocabulary becomes part of ocoeco's language: a vocabulary table (term, means, not, see), the shared words defined by ocoeco itself, a project's own words beside them, translated like everything else, and shown in views.
rejected: Folding definitions into the concepts table; a glossary written by the observatory about projects.
why: Asked for by the author, so the work can be spoken about clearly; concepts and vocabulary answer different questions.

decision: Where the whole is weakest right now is where attention goes.
rejected: triage (medical jargon); focus; priorities (a ranking someone sets)
why: What should be looked at next, read from every project - not what is loudest.

decision: An idea a project rests on, with why it matters, is a concept.
rejected: principle (a rule to follow, a narrower thing); belief
why: Distinct from idea (why the project exists) and from vocabulary (what a word means).

decision: A shared process that projects call, not copy, is a conveyor.
rejected: pipeline (CI jargon, and one run); template (copied, the opposite)
why: A conveyor carries any load the same way; you put work on it, you do not build your own.

decision: A lens chosen to stand in the observatory's navigation is curated.
rejected: featured, pinned (web jargon); official (claims an authority it does not have)
why: Says chosen with care, and nothing more; any lens is still found without it.

decision: An owned fork pinned upstream and changed only as patches meant to go home is a cutting.
rejected: fork (suggests drifting apart); vendored copy (a frozen copy, nothing goes home)
why: Rhizoid's gardening word: a cutting is a living piece of the parent plant, grown in your soil.

decision: A choice taken, with why and what was rejected, is a decision.
rejected: ADR (an acronym a reader must be taught); choice (says nothing of the alternatives)
why: The plain word; the rejected options are what make it worth keeping.

decision: Minutes weighted by load are effort.
rejected: cost (money); toil score (jargon); workload (NASA-TLX's wider measure)
why: Effort is the plain word for time and strain together - the 30 kg box.

decision: A project's whole chain on one page is its essence.
rejected: overview, summary (say less, not more); dashboard (numbers, no reasons); at a glance
why: Essence is what a thing most truly is; the page shows why, what, how and now at once.

decision: The daily job that writes down what a project's work produced is its gatherer.
rejected: collector (monitoring jargon); logger; recorder (plain, but breaks the metaphor)
why: One metaphor, kept whole: gatherers in each field, the harvest brought in by the observatory.

decision: The observatory's reading of every marked project is the harvest.
rejected: crawl, scrape (say how, not what); sync; import
why: It brings in what the gatherers gathered; the pair is easy to keep in mind.

decision: The three stretches of a path are horizons.
rejected: phase, stage (imply one ends before the next begins); level (sounds like a score)
why: Horizons are near and far at once - working, perfection and ongoing perfection are all in view together.

decision: Why a project exists, told for anyone, is its idea.
rejected: vision, mission (corporate jargon); pitch (selling); purpose (narrower)
why: The everyday word; a reader knows what an idea is without being taught.

decision: A grand view of a family of projects, declared as a small file, is a lens.
rejected: view (every page is a view - two meanings); dashboard; portal
why: You look through a lens; many lenses can look at the same commons, and anyone may make one.

decision: How draining an action was this time is its load.
rejected: exertion (formal); fatigue (an aftermath, not the act); difficulty
why: Short and physical, as in carrying a load; one number from Borg's CR10.

decision: The file by which a repository joins the commons is a mark.
rejected: manifest (a package's description elsewhere - two meanings); badge (a picture); tag (GitHub topics are only half of it)
why: Short and plain: a mark is something you put on a thing to say what it belongs to.

decision: A step on a path is a milestone, reached only when its evidence exists.
rejected: step (too small to name a stretch of work); goal (aims, not proves); checkpoint
why: The word readers know; the vocabulary adds only the rule that evidence reaches it, not a date.

decision: The mirror that reads and draws the commons is the observatory.
rejected: dashboard, portal, hub (suggest control)
why: One watches from an observatory and changes nothing: the mirror, not the control centre.

decision: The commons' language and machinery keep their own name, ocoeco.
rejected: a descriptive name (it is the name of a thing, not a description)
why: A proper name, chosen by the author: the observatory's ecosystem - the blood and heart.

decision: What a project must reach is its path.
rejected: roadmap (promises dates, a second meaning we do not want); plan; route
why: A path is walked step by step and says nothing of dates - exactly a list of milestones with their evidence.

decision: A repository with a mark is a project.
rejected: repository (says where, not what); module; component
why: The plain word everyone already uses; one repository, one project, one mark.

decision: The look around before acting is research.
rejected: prior art (the sources, not the looking); investigation; due diligence (legal)
why: The everyday word for looking into something before deciding.

decision: Manual work done often or heavily enough to ask for a tool is saturated.
rejected: overdue (blames); hot spot (jargon)
why: The author's own word; it says full - nothing more should be carried by hand.

decision: A work a project stands on is a source.
rejected: reference (also means a pointer); citation (the act, not the work)
why: The word readers know from any citation.

decision: The words a project speaks and exactly what they mean are its vocabulary.
rejected: glossary (a list at the back of a book); dictionary; terminology (formal)
why: A vocabulary is a language spoken - the ubiquitous language of domain-driven design - not a list kept at the back.

decision: What actually happens is work: the backlog, the log, what the gatherers record.
rejected: activity (only commits); progress (a judgment, not a record)
why: Plain, and set against the plan; the Essence page asks of it: what is happening now.

decision: How the steps are delivered and proven are its workings, as in the workings of a clock; a single entry is called by its kind.
rejected: working (unusual as a noun); means (plain, but it would collide with the vocabulary's own means field - one word, two meanings); mechanism (sounds like code only); instrument
why: Workings is everyday English for the parts that make something work. Working as a singular noun is unusual and was the weakest word in the language.

decision: Words are chosen like decisions: a vocabulary entry names the decision that chose it, the decision records the words rejected and cites research; every vocabulary is reviewed this way.
rejected: Definitions without reasons; leaving the words as they first came.
why: Asked by the author: wording is part of perfection. A word is how everyone after us will think about the thing.

decision: Six meanings, six signs: works, partly, broken or missing, not yet started, not known yet, not applicable. Planned work that has not started is shown calm and grey - never with the red of broken things.
rejected: Reusing the red sign for open backlog items.
why: Red on every planned item painted a project at the idea stage as a failure; like unknown, not yet is not a verdict.

decision: Words are laid out by the browser, never placed inside a drawing: SVG holds shapes only (and fixed-length marks the engine itself makes); every title and label is ordinary text in a cell of its own, shown whole, wrapping inside its cell; a row of cells scrolls sideways rather than squeezing.
rejected: Cutting titles at a fixed length; shrinking the font to fit; adjusting this one path by hand.
why: The path's milestone names were SVG text, which cannot wrap and knows nothing of its neighbours: they ran into each other, and cutting them at a fixed length only hid it until a longer title, a narrower screen or another language.

decision: Every project tells four things about itself, in its own data: its idea (why it exists, written by the project for anyone, as an ordered piece of writing), its path, its workings (how each step is delivered and proven, by which tools, and why we care), and its work. A lens gathers and shows these and writes none of them. The observatory is one more project that tells the same four.
rejected: How we work as one roof - a separate working set beside the projects (decided earlier the same day); the idea as terse cards written about a project.
why: From the author: how we work must not float beside the projects like a random toolbox - it belongs to each project, tied to its goals; and the idea must tell a commoner what this is, in the project's own voice. Shared tools are projects that others' workings name.

decision: The site is a designed static website from tad data - minimal, elegant, no JavaScript - not a tad text page.
rejected: Rendering tad's own pages for the observatory.
why: It is the observatory's visit card.

decision: Discovery is hexagonal; on GitHub the mark is the oco-project topic plus a kind topic, confirmed by oco.toml.
rejected: Code search for oco.toml (slow, rate-limited) as the primary way.
why: Topics are what GitHub's search indexes best: one query finds every marked repository.

decision: The observatory's engine (mark, discovery, harvest, site) is its own repository, in Rust; tad is to be rewritten in Rust with its formats unchanged.
rejected: Extending the Python tad renderer.
why: Sturdier machinery, compiled checks, one toolchain across the commons' tools.

decision: Essence is its own project - the method - beside ocoeco (the language it is written in) and ocoeco-engine (the eye that draws it). It must describe itself with nothing but itself, and be usable: a short guide with a test for each answer, and a measure of how completely any project tells its essence.
rejected: Essence as only a section of ocoeco's specification and a page of the engine; Essence as an essay with no check.
why: Proposed by the author: it gives why and how about how to do why and how. Weighed against the risk of one more box: the method is knowledge neither the format nor the renderer holds, and it is more general than software.

decision: Everything thought, decided and planned is written into the tad structure - concepts, decisions, backlog, session log, milestones - in the project it belongs to.
rejected: Prose documents alone; plans kept in conversation or memory.
why: Nothing may depend on anyone remembering.

decision: How we work is gathered under one roof, the creation-guidelines organization: the canon, the playbook, lab-agent (renamed lab-agent-oco), land and shot (moved from a personal repository), and the practices (moved from the observatory's own design data). Every practice names the tool or check that carries it; the share of practices so carried is its 'how close are we'. It is shown as a curated lens - think, do, tools - replacing the hard-coded page, and lab-agent-oco guide prints the whole working set. SUPERSEDED the same day by "a project, whole": how a project works belongs to each project, not to a roof beside them.
rejected: Leaving practices in the observatory's design data; a page of principles with no tools behind them; a new organization (the roof already exists).
why: Asked for by the author: a working and usable solution set, part of the grand picture, not a manifest. Two practices were broken on the day they were written, both resting on memory alone.

decision: The face uses Project Fluent message catalogs for its interface; projects keep data translations in a standard translations table (with by: human or machine), falling back to the source language; the site is rendered once per language under /<language>/ with identical paths, the root redirecting old addresses; the switcher is a thin line at the header's end naming each language in itself (English · Русский).
rejected: Plain string tables (wrong plurals); translated columns inside source tables; translating rendered HTML afterwards (fragile, no grammar); flags or bare codes in the switcher; switching by script or by the browser's language (no JavaScript, and a reader's choice should be theirs).
why: Fluent gets each language's grammar right (Russian has three plural forms); separate translation rows keep data made by work untouched; prefixes keep paths identical and old links alive.

decision: Grand views become lenses: repositories of their own that declare a family and its views as data; the observatory discovers and renders them all with one engine, curates some into its navigation and lists the rest as discovered. Our views become curated lenses built like any other; linux-phone-oco/docs keeps producing research data and the Linux Phones lens moves to its own repository in its family's organization.
rejected: Views hard-coded in the engine (a bottleneck and a gatekeeper); our views on a privileged path; a free-form template language for views (the vocabulary grows from real needs instead).
why: An observatory of a commons cannot be the only one allowed to look: views as data make the engine a general renderer, open to anyone's family of projects, with no privileged path.

decision: The observatory is a meta structure, tied to no project; its tabs are itself and the grand projects, each with its own views.
rejected: One flat set of tabs for everything.
why: A devices tab made the whole look device-centred; devices are one part of one grand project.

decision: The ecosystem of gathering, chaining and propagation is called ocoeco (observation commons observatory ecosystem).
rejected: Leaving it unnamed; the dashed form oco-eco.
why: It has become an information ecosystem, and deserves a name.

decision: New projects and organizations of the ecosystem may carry -oco in their names - a telling touch, not a requirement. Nothing existing is renamed: belonging is declared by the mark and shown by the topic.
rejected: -oco added to every existing organization, repository, tool and command.
why: Agreed with the author after weighing it: a name that says where a thing belongs helps a person; but identity by name is the mistake Rhizome names, and renaming has real costs.

decision: ocoeco becomes its own repository and the working system from now on: the principle, the formats (tad is the format it speaks), gatherers, chaining, and the mark, discovery and harvest moved in from the observatory's engine, which keeps the face. tad-engine stays as it is, frozen, its formats unchanged.
rejected: Renaming tad-engine in place (its history and users are a different thing); keeping the machinery inside the observatory's engine.
why: The ecosystem's machinery belongs together and apart from the face; tad's name lives on as the format, keeping every existing file valid.

decision: The working practices are tad data in the observatory, and every agent reads them live through lab-agent guide.
rejected: Practices kept only in one agent's memory or in prose files that drift.
why: An improvement made once reaches every agent; no agent depends on its own memory to work well.

decision: Table columns are ranked best first from the data; unknown is shown as unknown and never counted as failure.
rejected: Hand-ordered columns; one 'how close' percentage that counted unknown as zero.
why: The order corrects itself as support grows; a gap in knowledge is not a verdict.

decision: tad is not a template but a rhizoid module (a rhizcut) supplied in every repository, with standard gatherers (CI jobs and hooks reading real files, tests, releases); tad has its own path, shown among the other projects rather than as a top tab.
rejected: tad as a template or a subtree copy; tad as a top tab.
why: Templates and copied subtrees drift and cannot send fixes back; tad is central but smaller than a grand aim like Linux Phones.

decision: Projects are shown against three horizons - working, perfection, ongoing perfection - on the readiness ladder, with milestones whose criteria are measured data.
rejected: A single progress bar; milestones ticked by hand.
why: Overall progress alone loses the reader; three honest horizons show where a project really stands.

decision: Hand-work is recorded on the way every change already goes: land asks for --hand ACTION or --no-hand, and a failure to record stops the landing.
rejected: A reminder nobody must answer; recording after the fact.
why: A ledger is only worth reading if it is never silently skipped; land is the one path every change takes.

decision: The harvest rebases its data onto whatever landed while it worked, and retries the push up to five times.
rejected: Pushing once and failing; force-pushing (would drop what landed); holding landings while a harvest runs.
why: Since land starts harvests, a change landing during a harvest's three minutes rejected its push (2026-11-11 14:45); the harvest writes only its own data/ files, so a rebase cannot collide with what lands.

decision: The lab machine holds an idle inhibitor while the agent serves jobs; it is updated through its package repository regularly.
rejected: Blocking sleep altogether - its owner may still put it to sleep on purpose.
why: It suspended on idle at 03:09 and the agent stayed stuck after waking until a reboot; and it stayed on lab-agent 0.1.39 for days because its package list was never refreshed.

decision: Everything breathes through ocoeco - its language, gatherers and checks - and the observatory stays a mirror: projects produce their data, the observatory reads it, and no project needs the observatory to work.
rejected: Projects depending on the observatory's site or harvest to function.
why: The author's direction that the whole lives through OCO, weighed against the risk of the mirror becoming a control centre and a single point of failure.

decision: No new Python, even for one-off glue: shell orchestrates, Rust carries the logic (rust-script for single files), repeated work becomes a Rust tool; tad stays as it is until ocoeco replaces it.
rejected: Python for throwaway glue; rewriting tad now.
why: Asked by the author: Python's ecosystem is fragile - versions, imports, strings. Measured on the lab machine: a rust-script one-off compiles once in seconds and then runs at once. The deeper cause of failed runs was text patching, answered by structured tools such as ocoeco note.

decision: land starts the observatory's harvest after merging a marked project; the harvest coalesces bursts - one run in progress, at most one waiting.
rejected: Each project's CI dispatching the harvest (a token with rights on the observatory in every project); harvesting every few minutes on a timer (wasteful when nothing changed).
why: Triggering the harvest and waiting for it was manual work done 19 times.

decision: Mechanical rules are enforced by the tools every change passes through, not kept as practices: land moves tags only onto what merged, checks changed workflows with actionlint and commit titles against the conventional form before pushing.
rejected: More practices; more care.
why: The author asked whether such things should be guarded by a tool rather than a mental note; twice in a day a practice did not hold.

decision: Whatever ships or is called by others is Rust; whatever repeats becomes a Rust tool; one-off glue in a job may stay small.
rejected: Python in shipped or shared code; rewriting every one-off line of glue.
why: Python let bugs reach runtime that a compiled language rules out; the record scripts that repeated became ocoeco note.

decision: tad stays the general substrate - a transparent database of text files in git - and is rewritten in Rust; ocoeco is one specific use built on it, and others (Truelink) will be. The wrap-up pass comes first; then tad in Rust is the focus.
rejected: Moving tad's duties into ocoeco and retiring tad (2026-11-11-wrap-up-then-tad, superseded: it would make a general tool specific); hardening tad's Python.
why: The author: tad is simple and general, and proved that a text/file database in git can be accessible, transparent and intelligible; ocoeco is a narrower use of it, and a coming idea (Truelink: facts, their sources and what is drawn from them, so fact-checking can be automated) needs tad too. Python leaves; tad does not.

decision: First a wrap-up pass settling every in-progress item; then the focus is moving tad's duties into ocoeco (declared table shapes, canonical form, documents rendered from data) and retiring tad's Python; phone work continues where it is not blocked.
rejected: Hardening tad in Python; dropping current work mid-way; switching before the board is honest. Superseded the same day by 2026-11-11-tad-in-rust: tad stays general, in Rust.
why: The author: big ideas wait on a backbone that is not Python, and loose ends make the whole hard to read. Making tad's Python pristine would polish what is being retired.

decision: Ingest talks to a small persistent daemon that keeps the analysis warm; reads against the store are a stateless command.
rejected: A fresh process for every call.
why: Loading and resolving a workspace is expensive and worth keeping warm; the daemon is the first instance of the later genome process.

decision: Structure is extracted with rust-analyzer's own semantic layer (ra_ap_hir), pinned, behind a stable SymbolGraph boundary; everything downstream speaks language-agnostic graph types.
rejected: The compiler's internals, MIR or a nightly-only interface; writing a parser or resolver.
why: Real name resolution as a library on stable Rust; the boundary insulates from its 0.0.x instability and is where another language's extractor plugs in.

decision: Graft - a closure turned back into compilable, running code - is in the first milestone.
rejected: Ending the first milestone at ingest, hash, store, sync.
why: If the structure cannot go back into something executable there is no point in it; proving the round trip first tests the representation before anything is built on it.

decision: The graph is the source of truth, without qualification; text is read once on the way in and emitted once on the way out.
rejected: Text as the content with structure as its index.
why: Describing it as 'a store of source text indexed by structure' quietly re-centres files - the old world with a hash bolted on.

decision: H(node) = blake3(postcard(hash form) ++ sorted references); local names replaced by positions; cycles condensed and hashed as one unit.
rejected: Hashing text; adding alpha-equivalence later.
why: Deterministic, structural, fast; alpha-equivalence built in from the start because it changes what the hash is.

decision: The kernel is not in the prototype; its only near-term role is the filesystem view, stages later.
rejected: Starting at the kernel.
why: 'Rust in the kernel' is an argument about timing, not a build target; kernel work is the slowest feedback there is.

decision: Sync is proven between two local stores before any network transport.
rejected: Starting with the network.
why: Deciding what to transfer is the part worth testing; the transport is mechanical after.

decision: Macros are expanded on the way in and not preserved as such.
rejected: Treating macros as something the graph must round-trip.
why: They are a convenience of text-based development; once the structure itself is edited they have no job.

decision: The project is Rhizome - a root system with no root, any point connecting to any point; its foundational engine is Hypha, the single filament; the tools are rz and hy. The substrate is the rhizome, definitions are nodes, a conjured shape is a shoot.
rejected: Alkahest; Aleph (taken); Mycorrhiza (the most exact, the hardest to spell).
why: Biology is load-bearing in the model, so the vocabulary comes from the same well.

decision: No new language: the host language's type system expresses boundaries and transformations.
rejected: A DSL.
why: Inventing a language to avoid using one was Nix's mistake.

decision: One shared store per machine (~/.local/share/hypha/store); a project holds only a hypha.lock - a small pointer file of closure roots.
rejected: A hidden .hypha per project, like .git.
why: A store per project would be isolated and non-deduplicating: the very thing the manifesto opens by attacking.

decision: The compiler is a black-box oracle at the single text boundary - today the only socket it has; Cranelift is the named long-term destination for code generation.
rejected: Treating the round trip through text as the destination.
why: It keeps the first milestone free of compiler engineering while naming where the text boundary finally disappears.

decision: Hypha is to be developed from its own graph, proven by a fixpoint: built from the graph, it ingests and re-emits itself to the identical hash. Files and git demote to a projection.
rejected: Keeping its own source in files for ever.
why: The field's answer to the trust hazard of self-hosting systems, and the hardest stress test for free.

decision: Each node keeps its verbatim source span beside its hash form; graft emits the original bytes, never a reconstruction.
rejected: Regenerating text from stripped structure.
why: Nothing is inferred on the way out; the structural hash is identity, the text a rendering of it.
